newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Canny investors can ride out EMU waves.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Canny investors can ride out EMU waves.

text.p: EMU concerns shuddered through European debt markets on Wednesday catching investors unawares and adding uncertainty to already faltering convergence plays.
But shrewd speculators can still bag sizeable returns by switching out of European high-yielders and into British gilts or U.S. Treasuries, economists said.

"Clearly investors want to take profits in these markets, but the problem in terms of switching out of Spain and Italy into Anglos is investors feel they've missed the currency rallies," said BZW European bond strategist Phyllis Reed.
"But that's no excuse -- people should be looking to hedge their exposure, and if they pick the right country and the right terms it can add to the attractions," Reed said.
Reports of an EMU entry compromise plan for Italy are the latest turn on the country's bumpy road to a single currency and may slow yield convergence with Bunds even more, analysts said.

But with Italian and Spanish five- and 10-year bond yields still below those of British gilts, switches into Britain coupled with currency hedges offer sound rewards, said Reed. "If you switch out of Italian five-years into five-year gilts, you pick up around 20 basis points," she said.
"If you hedge that three months forward, because Italian rates are still quite a way above UK three-month rates, you're adding around 100 basis points to that trade."
The trade gives a total hedge/yield pick-up of around 130 bps, a premium which could clearly go down to zero, Reed added.

Luca Jellinek, bond strategist from Paribas Capital Markets in London, said any postponement of Italy's entry into European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would likely benefit the long end of the Italian curve.
"And the short end has been overly penalised...so I would be in the short end and the long end and barbell that," he said.
Merrill Lynch European bond strategist Ifty Islam agreed there was value in the short end of the Italian curve.

"I don't think today's comments will change the view that the Bank of Italy has to cut interest rates," he said. "But the big problem in the near term is the weight of investor over- positioning in the shorter end of the Italian curve."
He said the expected curve steepening meant any weakness at the shorter end should be seen as a buying opportunity.
Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ, said markets would seek guidance from Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi's planned talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl about EMU on Friday.
"All these comments illustrate the deeply political nature on the whole project," he said.

Earlier, Prodi said Italy was "solemnly committed" to meeting the economic conditions for membership of EMU from the outset in 1999. He rejected reports Italy could be offered a deal to delay its entry as false, unjustified and unfounded. "They do nothing but generate uncertainty among Italians and on financial markets," he said.
Given the questions surrounding Italy's and Spain's place in a unified Europe, Reed also suggested switching from five-year Bonos into equivalent U.S. Treasuries.

"You can pick up around 40 basis points in the yield," said Reed. "But investors are worried about currency reversals, so you can hedge this exposure one month forward, because Spanish one-month rates are still higher than U.S one month rates."
Reed said the differential was around plus 72 basis points, giving a total yield/hedge pick up of around 112 basis points.
"There's a lot of value doing that," she said.
